why: The budget controller is a monotone readout along the delta, so a quarter dose buys a proportional part of the gain, with the length change arriving with it.
Half the controller dose recovers most of the budget-allocation gain, above linear interpolation (436), because the gain saturates before a = 1.
At three quarters dose the controller is nearly complete, so accuracy is close to RL's 463.
Extrapolating the controller makes answers converge earlier instead of running away, so accuracy drops only slightly below RL instead of collapsing.
At a = 1.5 the stronger stop/convergence readout ends answers cleanly, so few answers degrade into word-salad tails.
Length rises with the controller dose (more self-checking on short answers), so at a = 0.25 mean tokens rise above the cued base's 3,933 toward RL's 4,694.
Half dose nets about +37 over 410 plus resampling breaks of about 12, giving about 50 fixes among the base's 90 wrong problems.
Code-RL 3.1 was also trained with truncated rollouts as negatives, so it carries a budget controller (its delta also reads out deliberation tokens) and helps the cued base on math.
A random matched-norm difference carries no controller, so the cued base stays at its 410 level.
Without the controller direction the length profile is the cued base's, 3,933 tokens.
The base has no budget control: its wrong answers are its long ones (263 answers under 2,000 tokens, 13 wrong), so length predicts error strongly.
RL's change is a stop/deliberation readout, not math content, so few of the base-RL difference peaks sit at the first wrong step.
A low-rank stop/deliberation readout is close to a constant bias toward deliberation and against early stopping, so one vector per layer closes a sizeable share of the KL.
On RL text the decisive positions are more often deliberation or stop decisions, so the constant controller bias closes more.
RL's late layers read out deliberation words more often than the base's, at a few percent of positions.
The base reads out deliberation words less often than RL on the same text, at about half RL's rate or less.
